::: {.cite-bar .domain-intelligence}
[Partly expired]{.status .status-partly-expired} [Pub. L. 114-113]{.cite} [129 Stat. 2935]{.cite} [6 U.S.C. 1501-1510]{.cite}
:::

Enacted as Division N of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016. It set up a voluntary system for companies and the federal government to share cyber threat indicators and defensive measures, with legal protection for companies that take part.

## Key provisions

- Authorizes private entities to monitor their own systems and operate defensive measures.
- Protects companies from liability for sharing indicators in the manner the act prescribes.
- Requires removal of personal information not directly related to a threat before sharing.
- Makes the Department of Homeland Security the main civilian portal for receiving indicators.

## Why it matters

Not to be confused with the 2018 law that created the agency with the same initials. Its repeated lapses in 2025 and 2026 are a case study in how sunset clauses interact with the congressional calendar. It relies on the department created by the [Homeland Security Act](hsa-2002.qmd).

## Current status

Running on short extensions. The original ten-year term ended September 30, 2025 and the law lapsed twice before being extended through September 30, 2026. A continuing resolution then carried it into December 2026. A long-term renewal is tied to the FY2027 defense bill. Check current status.
